501: C is correct because Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed ingestion service that automatically loads streaming data into destinations such as an Amazon S3 data lake with no ongoing administration, while Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics analyzes the incoming payment data in real time. This combination is the most operationally efficient because both services are serverless and scale automatically to handle data arriving every minute. Other options require more management overhead or do not provide the same seamless real-time analysis plus automated delivery into S3.
502: C is correct because moving the website images to Amazon EFS provides a shared, highly available file system that can be mounted concurrently on every EC2 instance, eliminating the single-instance EBS dependency and improving both performance and storage resilience. E is correct because creating an AMI and provisioning instances behind an Application Load Balancer in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of two instances removes the single point of failure and improves performance through load distribution and automatic self-healing, while an Amazon CloudFront distribution caches the website content at edge locations to further accelerate delivery. Together these changes address both the performance and resilience requirements.
503: A is correct because an IAM role in the customer account with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch permissions and a trust policy to the company's account is the AWS-recommended cross-account access pattern. The company can assume the role through AWS STS to obtain temporary, short-lived credentials, so no long-term access keys need to be created, distributed, stored, or rotated. This provides least-privilege access without the credential-management risk that long-lived IAM user keys or stored Cognito credentials introduce.
504: C is correct because an AWS Transit Gateway acts as a central network hub that connects hundreds of VPCs across many accounts with a single attachment per VPC, which is far more operationally efficient than managing hundreds of individual VPC peering connections. Hosting the Transit Gateway in the networking team's dedicated AWS account also centralizes network governance. Configuring static routes from each VPC to the Transit Gateway enables any-to-any connectivity with minimal route administration.
505: C is correct because Spot Instances offer discounts of up to 90 percent compared to On-Demand pricing, making them the most cost-effective choice for nightly batch workloads. The requirement that a failed job is simply reprocessed by another instance makes the workload fault tolerant and interruption tolerant, which is exactly the profile that Spot Instances are designed for. Scaling out based on CPU usage ensures enough capacity exists to complete the jobs within the 12:00 AM to 6:00 AM window.
506: C is correct because generating Amazon S3 presigned URLs allows files to be uploaded directly from the user's browser into an S3 bucket, completely offloading the upload traffic from the application servers. This is the most scalable solution because S3 can absorb virtually unlimited concurrent uploads, so the website can handle spikes during large events without any server infrastructure growing to match demand. The presigned URLs also keep the uploads secure without exposing the bucket publicly.
507: A is correct because Amazon DynamoDB global tables maintain a single, globally consistent table with automatic multi-Region replication, so every Regional deployment can use its local Regional endpoint while reading and writing the same logically central reservation database. DynamoDB global tables deliver single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale, which keeps average update latency well under the 1-second requirement. Each Regional web deployment remains separate while the reservation data stays globally consistent without custom synchronization logic.
508: B is correct because an EC2-backed AMI lifecycle policy automatically creates tagged AMI backups on the twice-daily schedule and can be configured to automatically copy the images to the us-west-2 Region, meeting the automation and disaster recovery requirements with minimal administrative effort. D is correct because AWS Backup provides a fully managed, tag-based backup plan that can be scheduled to run twice daily and configured with a cross-Region copy destination of us-west-2, automating both the backup and the DR copy in one policy. Both solutions keep data loss under 24 hours and eliminate manual, on-demand copy steps.
509: B is correct because network ACLs are stateless and support explicit deny rules, so adding an inbound deny rule for the offending IP addresses to the web tier subnets immediately blocks the illegitimate requests at the subnet boundary before they consume resources. Security groups cannot contain deny rules, which rules out the security-group based options. Blocking the malicious traffic at the network ACL resolves the immediate performance problem while the company investigates a permanent solution.
510: C is correct because a VPC peering connection between the ap-southeast-2 VPC and the eu-west-1 VPC provides a private, encrypted path for cross-Region communication once the subnet route tables are updated with the peering routes. Because security groups cannot reference security group IDs across an inter-Region peering connection, the database security group must allow traffic from the eu-west-1 application server IP addresses, which is exactly what this option does. This design keeps the traffic secure and private over the AWS global backbone rather than the internet.
511: C is correct because Amazon Aurora Serverless (On-Demand PostgreSQL-compatible) automatically starts up, scales capacity, and shuts down based on actual demand, and you pay only per second while the database is active. Since each development environment is used only about half of the 8-hour workday, on-demand billing avoids paying for provisioned capacity that sits idle the rest of the time. Always-on Aurora or RDS instances would bill continuously even when the environments are not in use, making them less cost-effective.
512: A is correct because AWS Config can continuously audit and identify resources that are not tagged, and once those resources are tagged programmatically, the AWS Backup plan can use those tags to automatically include all AWS resources in backups. This approach automates resource discovery, tagging, and backup coverage with the least manual effort. The other options either require ongoing manual reviews by account owners or do not feed resources into the backup plan at all.
513: A is correct because hosting a static website in Amazon S3 and invoking AWS Lambda to resize the uploaded images creates a fully serverless architecture that is highly available and scales automatically with unpredictable traffic. S3 durably serves the static content while Lambda scales concurrently with incoming resize requests, and an S3 bucket provides durable image storage. This design maximizes scalability with no capacity planning or server management required.
514: B is correct because when the Amazon EKS control plane has public endpoint access disabled, the worker nodes in the private subnets have no internet path to reach the cluster's private Kubernetes API endpoint. Creating interface VPC endpoints allows the nodes to connect to the control plane entirely over the private AWS network, which is what enables them to join the cluster while still satisfying the security compliance requirement of endpoint private access set to true and public access set to false.
515: B is correct because Amazon Redshift supports both client-side and server-side encryption, including encryption at rest and in transit for data warehouse workloads. C is correct because Redshift clusters can be paused and resumed, so the company can build analytics workloads during specified hours when the application is not active and avoid paying for compute when the cluster is idle. E is correct because Redshift is a petabyte-scale data warehouse whose RA3 managed storage and concurrency scaling allow it to elastically scale to very large datasets and very high request volumes per minute.
516: B is correct because Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda is a fully serverless compute option that removes all infrastructure management, giving it the least operational overhead. Provisioned concurrency keeps a pool of initialized Lambda execution environments continuously warm and ready to respond immediately, which guarantees consistent low latency even during the peak usage times of the year. This meets the latency and predictability requirements without provisioning or managing servers, containers, or clusters.
517: A is correct because Amazon Systems Manager Session Manager natively supports sending session logs directly to an Amazon S3 bucket, which can be enabled in the Systems Manager console by simply choosing the destination bucket for the session data. This requires no agents, custom documents, scheduled jobs, or additional pipelines, making it the most operationally efficient solution. The alternative approaches introduce unnecessary moving parts such as CloudWatch agents, log subscriptions, or EventBridge schedules.
518: A is correct because RDS storage autoscaling automatically increases the allocated storage when free space runs low, without any downtime or manual intervention. Once enabled, Amazon RDS monitors disk usage and grows the volume as needed, which requires the least effort compared to manually resizing the instance, changing the storage type, or performing a backup, increase, and restore migration.
519: B is correct because AWS Service Catalog is designed to let an organization centrally create, manage, and deploy a curated portfolio of approved products, such as packaged solutions and tools, that customers can provision in a governed self-service manner. This gives the consulting company central management of a common set of solutions while still allowing customers worldwide to deploy them on demand. The other options do not provide this centralized catalog-and-self-service model.
520: B is correct because DynamoDB on-demand mode instantly accommodates unpredictable application traffic by automatically scaling read and write capacity up and down as demand changes, with no capacity planning required. For a workload with moderate-to-high and unpredictable throughput, on-demand billing avoids both throttling from under-provisioned tables and wasted spend on over-provisioned tables, making it the most cost-effective configuration here. The Standard table class is also the right choice because the data is accessed continuously by the application rather than infrequently.
